introduction-one-ip-one-server.core: Normally an IP address identifies one interface in one place (unicast). Anycast announces the same IP prefix from many locations, and BGP delivers each packet to the topologically nearest one. Clients see one address, the network picks the site. That makes anycast the backbone of global DNS, CDNs and DDoS protection.

first_principles.problem: A global service with a single IP in Virginia gives Asian users 250 ms round trips.
truths: The same prefix can be announced from many places.

analogy.title: A chain store with one phone number
analogy.story: Call the number anywhere and you reach the nearest branch automatically.
analogy.breaks: Phone routing is geographic; BGP nearness is topological.

example.title: Same IP, different sites
flow: From São Paulo: 1.1.1.1 → GRU PoP (4 ms)

check.q: How does a client choose which anycast site to reach?
check.a: It doesn't; the internet's BGP routing delivers packets to the topologically nearest announcing site.

how-it-works-bgp-trickery.core: Each anycast site runs routers that announce the shared prefix (usually a /24 for IPv4, the smallest widely accepted) to local transit and peers. Upstream networks see multiple paths with different AS_PATHs and pick their best, which typically means the nearest site. Health checks drive announcements: if a site's service fails, a BGP daemon withdraws the route and traffic shifts to other sites within seconds.

first_principles.problem: A site's DNS servers crash but the router keeps announcing the prefix, black-holing nearby users.
derivation: Announce a **/24 (or /48 v6)** from each site.
Run **BGP on service hosts** (ExaBGP, BIRD) or routers.

analogy.title: Shops turning their 'open' sign on and off
analogy.story: If a shop closes, its sign goes off and customers automatically go to the next nearest.
analogy.breaks: Customers read signs instantly; BGP convergence takes seconds to minutes.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ExaBGP process: announce while local DNS answers
import subprocess, sys, time
up = None
while True:
    ok = subprocess.run(['dig', '+time=1', '@127.0.0.1', 'health.example'], capture_output=True).returncode == 0
    if ok != up:
        verb = 'announce' if ok else 'withdraw'
        sys.stdout.write(f'{verb} route 192.0.2.0/24 next-hop self\n'); sys.stdout.flush()
        up = ok
    time.sleep(2)

check.q: Why do anycast deployments typically announce /24s?
check.a: Many networks filter IPv4 prefixes longer than /24, so a /24 is the smallest prefix reliably propagated.

benefit-1-latency-reduction.core: Latency is bounded by the speed of light in fibre, about 200 km per ms, plus routing detours. Serving from a site 50 km away instead of 8,000 km cuts round trips from ~100 ms to a few ms. Every TCP and TLS handshake and every DNS lookup multiplies the saving, so anycast PoPs that terminate connections near users speed up the whole interaction, not just the first byte.

first_principles.problem: A login flow with DNS, TCP, TLS and three API calls takes 1.2 s for distant users, mostly waiting on round trips.

analogy.title: Local bank branches
analogy.story: Multiple short trips to a nearby branch beat a single trip to the head office in another country.
analogy.breaks: Bank trips are sequential human time; network RTTs add up silently.

example.title: Round-trip math
flow: DNS + TCP + TLS 1.3 + request ≈ 4 RTT = 360 ms

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Hundreds of ms saved per interaction.

check.q: Why does edge TLS termination help even for uncached dynamic content?
check.a: The multiple handshake round trips happen over a short distance, and the edge reuses a warm connection to the origin.

benefit-2-ddos-mitigation.core: With anycast, attack traffic from a global botnet is split across every site by BGP: each PoP absorbs only the bots in its catchment. Combined capacity (hundreds of Tbps for large providers) dwarfs any single site, and a saturated site can withdraw while others keep serving. That's why DNS roots, Cloudflare and scrubbing services all use anycast.

first_principles.problem: A 1 Tbps DDoS overwhelms a single 100 Gbps data centre, but the attacker can't concentrate it on one site of a 300-PoP anycast network.

analogy.title: Many small dams instead of one big one
analogy.story: A flood spread across many rivers is absorbed; concentrated on one, it breaks the dam.
analogy.breaks: Floods follow terrain; attackers can try to target specific catchments.

check.q: Why must the origin IP stay hidden behind an anycast DDoS service?
check.a: Attackers who learn it can bypass the anycast network and hit the origin directly.

the-catch-tcp-state-and-route-flapping.core: Anycast is ideal for stateless UDP (DNS), but TCP connections hold state on one server. If a BGP change shifts a client's packets to another site mid-connection, that site has no state and sends RST, breaking the session. Route flaps, ECMP differences and load-balancer hashing can all cause this. Mitigations are stable announcements, consistent hashing within sites, short-lived connections, and QUIC connection IDs.

first_principles.problem: Large downloads from an anycast CDN occasionally fail with resets when internet routes shift.
truths: TCP state lives on one host.
Other sites don't share that state.
derivation: Use **anycast for entry**, unicast for long sessions.

analogy.title: Switching call centres mid-call
analogy.story: If the network reroutes you to a different centre mid-conversation, the new agent has no idea who you are.
analogy.breaks: Agents can ask to start over; TCP just resets.

example.title: Hybrid pattern
flow: Large downloads redirected to unicast PoP IP

check.q: Why is anycast a natural fit for DNS but trickier for long TCP sessions?
check.a: DNS queries are short stateless UDP exchanges; TCP sessions break if routing shifts packets to a site without the connection state.

anycast-vs-geodns-choosing-the-right-too.core: Anycast steers at the network layer: one IP, BGP chooses, failover in seconds, superb DDoS absorption, but you need your own ASN and prefixes (or a provider) and get coarse control. GeoDNS steers at the DNS layer: different IPs per location, fine-grained policies such as data residency and weights, and works with any servers, but it's slowed by DNS TTLs and resolver location errors. Many platforms combine them.

first_principles.problem: A team must choose between anycast and GeoDNS for a new multi-region API.
truths: Network-layer steering is fast and coarse.
DNS-layer steering is flexible and cached.
Requirements differ: residency, failover speed, DDoS.

analogy.title: Automatic call routing vs a receptionist
analogy.story: The phone network routes the call to the nearest office automatically (anycast); a receptionist decides by caller details (GeoDNS).
analogy.breaks: Receptionists can be updated instantly; DNS answers are cached.

example.title: Decision
flow: Multi-region SaaS → GeoDNS + per-region anycast LBs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each requirement mapped to the right tool.

check.q: Which approach suits strict data-residency requirements better?
check.a: GeoDNS, because it explicitly maps client locations to specific regional endpoints, whereas anycast follows BGP paths you don't fully control.
